title: Amazon SageMaker notebooks now support trusted identity propagation
summary: Discover more about what's new at AWS with Amazon SageMaker notebooks now support trusted identity propagation
body_text: Amazon SageMaker Notebooks now support Trusted Identity Propagation (TIP) with Amazon Athena, Amazon Redshift, and Amazon EMR Serverless, enabling per-user access control for data analytics. When connected to a TIP-enabled compute in a TIP-enabled Project, each notebook user's IAM Identity Center identity flows through to AWS Lake Formation, ensuring they see only the tables, columns, and rows their permissions allow, without sharing a single broad execution role. With TIP, enterprises get per-user data boundaries enforced based on who is running the query, full audit attribution with CloudTrail recording which user accessed data, and reduced admin friction since identity propagates automatically through the existing compute connection with no extra login, token, or role management required. To get started, use a notebook in a TIP enabled Project with the supported engines. This feature is available in all AWS Regions where Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio is available . To learn more, see Trusted identity propagation in the Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio Administrator Guide and Notebooks in the Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio User Guide.

title: Whole-Genome Sequencing With Mito Health: What to Know
summary: Mito Health now offers whole-genome sequencing through Genome Computer. Learn why your genome is a durable genetic baseline, how it fits with preventive care, and what to expect.
body_text: Most health data is a snapshot. Your bloodwork captures what is happening right now. Your sleep score reflects last night. Your VO2 max, body composition, glucose, hormones, inflammation, and nutrient markers all move as your life moves. That is exactly why Mito tracks them. The body changes, and good preventive care should change with it. Your genome is different. It is the baseline you are born with. It does not tell the whole story of your health, but it gives you a permanent layer of context that can sit underneath everything else you measure. It can help explain why two people respond differently to the same lifestyle, the same medication, the same diet, or the same risk factor. It can also become more useful over time as genomic science improves. That is why Mito Health is adding whole-genome sequencing to the preventive health stack. Members can now access whole-genome sequencing at two sequencing depths: 3x whole-genome sequencing and 30x whole-genome sequencing . Both options read across your whole genome rather than checking a fixed list of genotyping-array sites. The goal is simple: give you durable ownership of your genetic data, then help you use it responsibly as one part of a broader health picture. Why Genome Data Belongs in Preventive Health Preventive health works best when you can see risk early enough to act. Bloodwork can show whether inflammation is rising, ApoB is high, glucose regulation is drifting, or iron stores are low. Imaging can reveal structural findings before symptoms appear. A microbiome test can add context about digestion, inflammation, and gut ecology. Medical history shows what has already happened to you and your family. Genome data adds another layer: inherited context. It can help explain predispositions that were already present before your first lab draw. For some people, that context is about common traits. For others, it is about inherited risk, carrier status, or how their body may process certain medications. For everyone, it is a long-lived data layer that can be revisited as interpretation improves. That last point matters. Sequencing your genome is not only about what can be interpreted today. It is also about owning the raw material for future interpretation. Scientific understanding changes. Variant databases improve. New research links genetic patterns to new clinical questions. A genome file you control can be reanalyzed later without starting from zero. What Makes Our Whole-Genome Sequencing Different Many consumer DNA products use genotyping arrays. Those tests look at a selected set of known sites across the genome. They can be useful for ancestry, traits, and some common variants, but they are not the same as sequencing the genome itself. Whole-genome sequencing reads across your DNA more broadly. The CDC describes whole-genome sequencing as the largest genetic test because it looks at all of a person’s DNA, not just genes or a preset panel of variants. That breadth is why whole-genome sequencing is a more durable foundation. It is not limited to the questions a chip was designed to answer. It can support many kinds of future analysis, from common variant interpretation to more clinically oriented review when the sequencing depth is high enough and the interpretation is handled appropriately. In plain English: a genotyping array is a checklist. Whole-genome sequencing is closer to owning the source material. Why Mito Is Launching This Now Mito’s view of health has always been systems-based. No single marker explains a person. ApoB matters, but so do inflammation, insulin resistance, blood pressure, sleep, nutrition, fitness, family history, and the care plan that ties those signals together. We built Mito around that idea: give members access to better data, then make it usable with longitudinal tracking, AI-supported analysis, and clinician oversight where it matters. Genome data fits naturally into that model. It is not a replacement for bloodwork. It is not a shortcut around clinical care. It is not a magic answer key. It is context. For example, if someone has persistently high LDL cholesterol or ApoB, genome data may add context about inherited lipid risk. If someone is considering a medication, pharmacogenomic findings may be worth discussing with a clinician. If someone is planning a family, carrier information may matter. If someone wants to understand ancestry-linked or trait-linked patterns, the common-variant layer can make the information more personal. The value comes from combining layers. Your genome may explain predisposition. Your biomarkers show what is actually happening now. Your habits, environment, and care plan determine what changes next. What You Can Learn Mito’s launch includes two whole-genome sequencing options. The 3x depth is a light read across the whole genome. It is best for the common-variant layer: ancestry, traits, polygenic scores, and exploratory genome ownership. The 30x depth is the clinical-grade depth. It includes the common-variant layer and adds stronger confidence for rare and pathogenic variants, carrier status, ClinVar-linked findings, and pharmacogenomics. Depth drives confidence. If your primary goal is health-oriented genome data, 30x is usually the stronger choice. If your goal is exploration, ancestry, traits, and owning a whole-genome file at a lower price, 3x can make sense. Ownership Matters The most important shift is not just that genome sequencing is becoming more accessible. It is that people should be able to own their own data. Your genome should not be trapped in a one-time report. It should not disappear behind a dashboard that only answers today’s questions. It should be portable, downloadable, and useful beyond the first interpretation. That is why raw genome files matter. A static report can become outdated. A genome file can be reinterpreted. As new tools, databases, and clinical standards emerge, the same underlying data can support new questions. We wrote more about this ownership principle in Your Genome Should Stay Yours , including why genomic data needs stronger control than ordinary health data. This is also why privacy and control matter. Genetic data is deeply personal. Before ordering any genome product, you should understand what data is generated, where it is stored, what files you can download, how deletion works, and what the provider does or does not do with your information. Genome Computer publishes its current privacy and ordering model in its public FAQ. What Genome Sequencing Cannot Do The responsible version of genome sequencing starts with limits. Your genome does not determine your destiny. Most common diseases are shaped by many genes plus environment, behavior, age, exposures, and chance. A risk signal is not a diagnosis. A low-risk result is not immunity. A variant may be important, uncertain, benign, or meaningful only in a specific clinical context. Genome data should not be used alone to make medical decisions. That is not fine print. It is central to using this data well. The CDC notes that direct-to-consumer genetic test results should not be used alone for treatment or medical-care decisions. ClinGen also states that ClinVar information is not intended for diagnostic use or medical decision-making without review by a genetics professional. This is the standard Mito will keep reinforcing: use genome data as powerful context, not as a standalone verdict. The Future Is Longitudinal The first era of consumer DNA was curiosity. Where did my ancestors come from? What traits do I carry? What can a handful of variants tell me? The next era is longitudinal. Your genome should sit alongside your labs, imaging, microbiome, medical history, medications, family history, and goals. It should help personalize preventive care over years, not generate a one-time novelty report. That is the direction Mito is building toward. We want members to understand their health with more depth and less guesswork. Sometimes that means tracking a biomarker over time. Sometimes it means finding the right screening test. Sometimes it means bringing inherited context into a clinician conversation. Sometimes it means knowing what not to over-interpret. Whole-genome sequencing gives members a new layer of self-knowledge. Used carefully, it can make the rest of your health data more personal. Your genome is not the whole map. But it is one of the few health assets you only need to sequence once, can own for life, and can keep learning from as science moves forward. Explore Whole-Genome Sequencing With Mito Mito members can now explore: 3x whole-genome sequencing for ancestry, traits, polygenic scores, and whole-genome ownership. 30x whole-genome sequencing for clinical-grade depth, rare and pathogenic variant confidence, carrier status, ClinVar findings, and pharmacogenomics. If you are choosing between them, start with your goal. For exploration, 3x is a real entry into whole-genome sequencing. For health-oriented use, 30x is the stronger default. Either way, the bigger shift is ownership. Your genome is a health asset. Now it can be part of the same preventive health system you use to understand the rest of your body. References Genome Computer FAQ CDC: Genetic Testing ClinGen: ClinVar

title: How to Get Emails Out of Spam and Stay in the Inbox
summary: Learn how to get emails out of spam with provider-specific fixes, authentication checks, and long-term reputation strategies that keep you in the inbox.
body_text: To get emails out of spam, the fastest fix is to mark the message as not spam in the recipient mailbox, move it to the inbox, and create a filter so trusted mail stays out of spam. Then the sender has to fix SPF, DKIM, and DMARC , reduce volume to engaged recipients, and rebuild reputation with controlled sending. That order matters because inbox providers use complaint rate , engagement, and authentication as reputation signals, and Gmail warns when complaints rise above 0.1% , with active penalization starting above 0.3% Sender guidance on spam complaints and recovery . Much advice skips straight to subject lines and content tweaks, but that's usually noise when the problem is mailbox classification, a broken technical setup, or reputation decay. Immediate Steps to Rescue Emails from Spam The first move is to correct the mailbox's classification. In Gmail, open the message in Spam, choose Not spam , then move it to the inbox and create a filter that applies Never send it to spam for that sender or thread Gmail spam recovery steps . That action does more than rescue one message, it gives the provider a direct signal that the mail is wanted. What recipients should do right away The same principle applies across major providers, even if the button labels change. In Outlook and Yahoo, the practical goal is the same, move the message out of junk, mark it as safe or not junk, and let the mailbox learn from the correction. The mailbox is part of the fix. If the user keeps clicking spam, the provider keeps learning the wrong thing. For senders, this is the right support script to share with customers or prospects who say they are missing messages: Open the spam or junk folder: Find the missing email thread first, then act on that exact message. Mark it as not spam: This retrains the mailbox model for that sender and thread. Move it to the inbox: That reinforces the classification change. Create a filter or safe-sender rule: This gives trusted mail a durable path forward. A one-time rescue helps only that thread. A filter is the durable fix because it prevents the same sender from being misfiled again. That said, whitelisting alone won't solve a sender problem if the domain identity, authentication, or engagement pattern still looks weak. The inbox can be retrained, but the sender still has to earn trust. Diagnosing Why Your Emails Land in Spam The quickest way to waste time is to treat every spam issue like a content problem. In practice, the failure usually sits in one of three places, mailbox classification, authentication gaps, or reputation decay. Each one calls for a different fix, and using the wrong fix usually leaves the underlying issue in place. The three-way triage Mailbox classification issues are the easiest to recognize when a message lands in spam even though the recipient wanted it. The rescue step above often works here, because the problem sits partly with the user and partly with the provider's filtering model. Authentication gaps are different. If the domain sends without a clean SPF, DKIM, and DMARC setup, providers have less reason to trust the message Twilio deliverability guidance and DMARC rollout guidance . That is a sender-side issue, not a content issue. Reputation decay shows up when the mail is technically valid and still gets filtered. That usually means too many complaints, too much sending to inactive recipients, or sending patterns that look abrupt or careless. Symptom What it usually suggests First move Message is misfiled for an engaged recipient Mailbox classification issue Ask the user to mark it not spam Authentication checks are incomplete Technical configuration gap Fix SPF, DKIM, DMARC Opens, replies, and engagement are fading Reputation decay Reduce volume and send only to engaged contacts Mailbox providers reward sustained positive engagement and punish repetitive low-response sends. Outreach guidance says to keep complaint rates low, cap follow-ups, and stop sending to non-responders because negative engagement accumulates over time Outreach best practices . That is the key diagnostic clue. If the audience stopped engaging, the inbox will notice. Practical rule: If the message is wanted but misfiled, fix the mailbox. If the sender identity is weak, fix authentication. If engagement is falling, fix the audience and the sending pattern. How to read the signals Bounce messages help separate deliverability issues from spam placement issues. A hard bounce means the address is bad and should be removed. A soft bounce, repeated complaints, or a drop in engagement points to a broader reputation problem. Google Postmaster Tools, Sender Score, and Talos are useful because they show whether the sender is losing trust before inbox placement collapses metrics and reputation monitoring guidance . The goal is not to watch every metric. The goal is to identify which lever to pull first. Fixing Email Authentication for SPF DKIM and DMARC Authentication is the first thing I check when a sender keeps landing in spam despite clean content and a decent list. Mailbox providers want proof that a message really comes from the domain it claims to use, and SPF, DKIM, and DMARC are treated as baseline setup, not optional extras. If those signals are missing or broken, every other fix has less room to work. What each record does SPF tells providers which servers are allowed to send on behalf of the domain. DKIM adds a digital signature so the message can be checked for tampering. DMARC connects those signals and tells providers how to handle a failure. A clean setup matters more than a polished campaign. One broken record can make a legitimate sender look unreliable, even when the content is sound and the list is healthy. Common mistakes that break trust Authentication problems usually come from sloppy setup, not technical mystery. Multiple SPF records, misaligned DKIM selectors, and rushed DMARC enforcement can all confuse mailbox providers. The safer path is gradual rollout. Start with a monitoring policy such as p=none , confirm that legitimate traffic is passing, then tighten enforcement only after you know what is being authenticated. That staged approach is boring, and boring is good in deliverability. Here's the practical order: SPF first: Confirm only approved senders are using the domain. DKIM second: Make sure messages are signed correctly. DMARC third: Monitor before enforcing, then tighten carefully. A clean technical setup does not rescue a dead list, but without it, everything else is harder. That is why a deliverability audit should start with authentication before touching subject lines or templates. For teams setting up the full stack, this DKIM, SPF, DMARC, and BIMI setup guide is a useful reference for checking the basic plumbing. Rebuilding Sender Reputation Through Warmup and Engagement Authentication gets the door open. Reputation decides whether the mail gets invited in. title: Closing a Critical Safety Gap in Autonomous Driving
summary: Learn how Cerence EVD uses Audio AI to detect emergency vehicles and alert drivers and autonomous systems to approaching sirens, enhancing safety for all road users.
body_text: Autonomous mobility is on the rise. Robotaxi companies like Zoox and Waymo are serving hundreds of thousands of rides each week, autonomous trucking is advancing toward widescale commercial deployment, and automated driving systems continue to expand across passenger vehicles and commercial fleets. As these technologies mature, attention is increasingly turning to one question: how safely can autonomous vehicles (AVs) operate in complex, real-world conditions? One of the most important aspects of this conversation is how AVs recognize and respond to emergency vehicles. To help address this challenge, Cerence AI developed Emergency Vehicle Detection (EVD), an audio AI solution that detects approaching emergency vehicles and alerts either the driver or the vehicle system. The Safety Challenge Emergency situations are rarely straightforward. An ambulance may be approaching from behind in heavy traffic. A fire truck may be navigating through a congested urban corridor. First responders may be managing an active scene using emergency lights, traffic cones, and other signals. In July, the United States National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) issued a public call to action urging autonomous vehicle developers to place greater focus on interactions between AVs and first responders. The agency highlighted repeated instances where AVs interfered with emergency operations. The implications extend beyond autonomous driving . Whether operated by a human or an automated system, a car that fails to recognize an approaching emergency vehicle can delay response times, create confusion in already stressful situations, and introduce unnecessary safety risks. As automated mobility continues to scale , emergency vehicle awareness will become an increasingly important component of the overall safety stack. Why Audio Matters Many autonomous driving conversations focus on what a vehicle can see. Cameras, radar, and other sensors provide essential information about the surrounding environment. Yet emergency vehicles are often heard before they are seen. Traffic, buildings, weather conditions, and other obstacles can limit visibility. Sirens are specifically designed to provide advance warning before an emergency vehicle reaches a driver's field of view. Those additional seconds give drivers or automated systems valuable time to make decisions that can impact safety-critical outcomes. Audio offers a unique and important layer of environmental awareness that complements other vehicle sensing technologies. Enabling Better Situational Awareness for Autonomous Vehicles Cerence EVD is certified in 47 countries and supports more than 1,500 siren sounds . It is designed to recognize a broad range of emergency vehicles, including ambulances, police cars, and fire engines. It can identify sirens from more than 300 meters away using vehicle-integrated microphones. When external microphones are used, detection distances can extend beyond 800 meters. External microphone configurations also support directional awareness, helping determine where the siren is coming from. Using advanced audio processing and AI-based classification, EVD can distinguish emergency sirens from surrounding sounds such as traffic noise, music, conversations, and other common driving distractions. Proven in Today's Vehicles and Tomorrow's Mobility Platforms Emergency vehicle detection is a real-world challenge that requires solutions capable of operating across countries, vehicle types, roadway conditions, and regulatory environments. Cerence EVD is already being deployed across vehicle programs and mobility platforms. Mercedes-Benz and BMW have integrated EVD as part of their automated driving initiatives, and the technology is being applied across use cases ranging from passenger vehicles to autonomous bus deployments. Cerence also works with customers across emerging mobility categories, including robotaxis and autonomous trucking . Looking Ahead As autonomous mobility continues to evolve , emergency vehicle awareness will become a foundational capability. Vehicles must be able to understand more than lane markings, traffic signals, and nearby objects. They also need to recognize critical situations developing beyond their immediate field of view and respond appropriately when every second counts. Cerence EVD has an important role to play in that future. Serving as a vehicle’s “ears,” it helps drivers recognize and respond to emergency vehicles earlier, supporting safer roads for drivers, passengers, first responders, and the communities they serve. Learn More To learn more about Cerence Emergency Vehicle Detection and how it can support your mobility platform, contact the Cerence AI team or visit the EVD page .

title: Best B2B Data Providers 2026: Comparison and Rankings
summary: Compare top B2B data providers for August 2026 across contact data, technographics, intent signals, and delivery formats to find the right fit.
body_text: Somewhere between signing a contract with a data provider and running your first campaign, a lot of teams realize the coverage is thin in their target segment, the delivery format doesn’t fit their stack, or the records are six months stale. That gap between the demo and reality is what this comparison is built to close. We’re breaking down the top B2B data providers for 2026 by the specifics that matter: data type, freshness, delivery method, and compliance posture. TLDR: B2B data providers supply raw data via API, flat files, webhooks, and Model Context Protocol (MCP) – your CRM or sales tool sits on top. B2B contact data decays at 22.5% per year, so a list clean 12 months ago is already a quarter wrong. Match the provider to your use case first: contact data, technographic signals, intent, firmographics, or job postings. Check delivery format, update cadence, and compliance sourcing before database size – large counts mask poor coverage. PredictLeads covers hiring, financing, and technology change signals, delivered via API, flat files, webhooks, and MCP. What Is a B2B Data Provider A B2B data provider collects, structures, and delivers information about businesses, including company profiles, contact records, technology usage, hiring signals, and news events, to sales, marketing, investment, and product teams. Instead of building a research team to track every account you care about, you buy access to a dataset that someone else has already crawled, cleaned, and organized. The provider handles the collection and structuring; you handle the decision about what to do with it. A data provider supplies the underlying information layer, not the interface you act on it through. A CRM, a sales engagement tool, or an outreach sequencer is where you use the data. The provider is where the data originates. Some companies blend the two by bundling raw data with a prospecting UI, but the function of a data provider is supply, not the tool built on top of it. Buyers tend to fall into one of two modes, and which one you are shapes which provider actually fits your needs. Data consumers read information through a tool they already use, such as a CRM field, a Clay enrichment column, or a dashboard built by someone else on the team. They care about accuracy, coverage, and whether the data shows up where they already work. Data builders integrate raw records through an API, flat files, webhooks, or MCP, usually to feed a scoring model, an internal tool, or a pipeline other systems depend on. They care about schema, freshness, and delivery format as much as the underlying facts. A sales rep filtering leads inside a CRM and a data engineer piping records into a warehouse are both buying B2B data, but they are shopping for different things. The rep wants clean fields that plug into an existing setup. The engineer wants documented endpoints, consistent schema, and a delivery method that fits how their pipeline already runs. Most provider comparisons treat these two buyers as interchangeable, which is why a tool that looks perfect in a demo can feel wrong the moment your team tries to use it. Before comparing vendors by name, decide which mode your team is in: consuming data through a tool you already have, or building a pipeline that other systems will depend on. Types of B2B Data Explained B2B data breaks down into five categories, and most providers specialize in one or two instead of covering all five well. Knowing which categories matter for your use case is the fastest way to cut a long list of vendors down to a handful worth trialing. Firmographic Data Firmographic data describes the company itself: name, headcount, industry classification, revenue range, location, and often a NAICS code. This is the layer almost every other dataset attaches to, since you need to know what a company is before you can filter or segment it. A CRM’s company fields, a market sizing exercise, or a due diligence memo all start here. Contact Data Contact data covers the people inside a company: names, titles, emails, and phone numbers. This is the layer most associated with the term “B2B database,” and the one that decays fastest, since people change jobs, titles shift, and emails go stale within months of being collected. Providers in this space compete mainly on match rate and how often records get refreshed. Technographic Data Technographic data identifies which software and tools a company runs, detected through website script tags, DNS records, job descriptions that list required skills, and other public signals. Sales teams use it to find accounts running a competitor’s tool or a complementary product, and marketing teams can use technology data to improve targeting. The detection method matters here: providers relying only on visible website tags miss tools that sit behind a login, while those pulling from job postings and DNS records tend to catch more of the stack. Intent Data Intent data tracks behavioral signals suggesting a company may be researching a purchase, often built from content consumption patterns across a network of publisher sites. It answers a different question than the other four categories: not who a company is or what it uses, but whether it appears to be in-market right now. Job Posting Data Job posting data covers active job openings, which reveal hiring priorities, growth areas, and where a company is putting budget. A company hiring for a security engineer signals a different buying window than one hiring for outbound sales reps, and the categories and seniority levels attached to each posting make that distinction easy to filter for. Top providers rarely stop at one category. A firmographic-only provider tells you what a company is but nothing about what it is doing right now, and a contact-only provider hands you names with no context for why to reach out. Vendors worth shortlisting tend to combine at least two or three of these categories, so rank which ones matter most for your workflow before comparing vendors by name. Top B2B Data Providers for 2026 The B2B data provider market splits into several distinct categories, and no single vendor covers all of them equally well. Contact database providers focus on verified emails and phone numbers for outreach. Intent data providers track buying signals like content consumption and search behavior. Technographic and signal providers monitor hiring, funding, and technology changes to time outreach. Company profile providers aggregate firmographic details for account research. Picking a vendor starts with identifying which of these problems you are actually solving. Provider Category Known For Delivery ZoomInfo Contact database Large verified contact volume for enterprise sales teams API, exports Apollo.io Contact database and outreach Combined prospecting and sequencing in one tool API, browser extension Cognism Contact database Compliance-focused coverage for EMEA-heavy sales motions API, exports Lusha Contact database Chrome extension prospecting for individual reps Browser extension, API Clearbit (Breeze Intelligence) Firmographic enrichment Form and CRM enrichment inside HubSpot API PredictLeads Technographic and signal data Hiring, financing, and technology change tracking across 123M+ companies, with structured signals for job openings, news events, and technographics sourced from script tags, DNS records, and job descriptions API, flat files, webhooks, MCP How to Choose a B2B Data Provider Picking a provider off a ranking list skips the part that actually matters: whether that provider fits how your team works. A few criteria apply regardless of category, and running any shortlist through them tells you more than a star rating ever will. Data quality and accuracy. Ask how a provider verifies records, beyond the raw count it claims to have. Some run automated matching against public sources, others rely on manual review, and a few just recrawl on a schedule and hope nothing changed. Decay rates matter here too: contact data goes stale fast, so a provider with no refresh cadence is selling you a shrinking asset from day one. Coverage and depth. A provider might claim tens of millions of companies, but if most of them sit in one country or one size bracket, that number tells you nothing about whether it covers your accounts. Check geographic reach, company size distribution, and industry concentration against your actual target list before comparing totals. Data freshness. Look for update cadences stated in days or weeks, not vague promises of continuous refresh. Timestamp fields on individual records let you filter by recency instead of trusting the vendor’s word for it, and historical data availability matters if you ever need to build trendlines instead of single snapshots. Compliance posture. GDPR and CCPA compliance should be a baseline requirement, not a selling point. SOC 2 certification signals a provider takes data security seriously beyond just legal compliance. If a vendor cannot explain where its data comes from, take that as a warning sign. Integration options. Match delivery to how your team actually works: a CRM connector if you live inside Salesforce or HubSpot, a documented API and webhooks if you are piping data into your own systems, flat file delivery if you are loading into a warehouse. A great dataset with no path into your workflow just sits unused. Pricing model. Seat-based pricing punishes teams that want to add users without adding budget. Credit-based and pay-as-you-go models scale with actual usage but require you to know your query volume ahead of time. Neither is inherently better, but mismatched pricing models are one of the more common reasons teams outgrow a vendor within a year. Free trial or sample data. A provider unwilling to let you test against a handful of your own target accounts before you commit is asking you to buy blind. Database size alone is a weak proxy for quality, and the market’s own growth proves it. The market for B2B sales data is on track to reach roughly $15 billion by 2030 , about 17 times its size in 2005, yet that growth in raw access has not translated into a matching gain in pipeline for most teams. The challenge has shifted from getting hold of contact data to using it before it goes stale, which is exactly why the criteria above matter more than the number printed on a provider’s homepage. Data Quality, Freshness, and the Cost of Bad Data Data quality is not a feature you can trade off against price. It is the difference between a dataset that makes your team faster and one that quietly wastes their week. The scale of the decay problem is worth sitting with. B2B data decays at 2.1 percent per month, or 22.5 percent annually, according to Cleanlist’s research on b2b data decay rates . Roughly one in four records in your CRM turns inaccurate every year without active maintenance, not because anyone did anything wrong, but because people change jobs, companies get acquired, and phone numbers get reassigned. Left unchecked, that decay compounds. A list that was clean 12 months ago is now a quarter wrong, and next year it will be worse. The cost of that decay is not abstract. Poor data quality costs US businesses 3.1 trillion dollars a year in wasted marketing spend, lost sales opportunities, and other inefficiencies. Translate that down to a single rep’s week and the pattern is familiar: emails that bounce, calls that reach a number reassigned to someone else, outreach sequences aimed at a company that already got acquired or quietly shut down six months ago. None of that shows up as a line item on an invoice, but it shows up in pipeline that never materializes and reps who stop trusting the tool. A dataset that cannot tell you when a record was last verified is asking you to trust it blindly. Good data hygiene is visible if you know where to look. A provider should be able to explain its verification method, and go further than reciting a company count. Source transparency matters here: knowing which URL, job posting, or DNS record produced a given detection lets you judge how reliable that signal actually is, instead of taking a black box match on faith. A few checks separate providers who take freshness seriously from those who paper over it: Update frequency stated per dataset. A company profile and a job posting do not decay at the same rate, and neither should be refreshed on the same schedule. A provider that lumps everything into one vague “regularly updated” claim is hiding the detail you need. Timestamp fields exposed at the record level. Fields like first_seen_at and last_seen_at let you filter for recency yourself instead of trusting a vendor’s claim of continuous refresh. Source-level provenance. Knowing whether a signal came from a job board, a press release, or a DNS record change tells you how much weight to put on it before you build a workflow around it. A provider that exposes those timestamps is handing you the tools to judge freshness on your own terms, not asking you to take its word for it. Teams building pipelines may also want to review how a technographic data API for B2B enrichment handles timestamp fields before committing. Compliance Requirements for B2B Data Assuming B2B data sits outside privacy law is no longer a defensible position. GDPR set the standard in 2018, and since then, CCPA and CPRA have expanded coverage in California, with 20 US states now carrying broad privacy laws on the books, according to Unify’s guide to b2b data compliance requirements . A contact record tied to a named person at a company counts as personal data under most of these frameworks, regardless of whether that person is acting in a business capacity. The penalties are not theoretical. GDPR fines have reached a cumulative total of 7.1 billion euros since enforcement began, and regulators have acted on complaints tied to purchased contact data, including B2B contact lists, well beyond consumer breaches. A vendor selling you a list does not absorb that risk on your behalf. You inherit it the moment you load those records into your CRM and start emailing or calling people on it. A few things are worth checking before you sign a contract, not after: GDPR and CCPA compliance posture. Ask for documentation, not a checkbox on a sales page. A provider that cannot describe its legal basis for processing contact data is a provider you should not trust with your list. Public-only sourcing. A provider that collects only publicly available information, from company websites, job postings, and public filings, carries a cleaner compliance story than one pulling from scraped or purchased lists of unknown origin. Deletion and opt-out handling. Ask how the provider processes a deletion request and how quickly that removal propagates to data you already downloaded. If a person opts out and the provider has no process for pushing that change to you, you are still holding a record you should not have. Security certifications. SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001 signal that a provider treats data handling as an audited practice, not an internal promise. Buying a contact list does not transfer the compliance burden away from you. It hands you the same obligations the provider had, minus the paperwork proving how the data was collected in the first place. Vetting a provider’s sourcing methodology is not a formality, it is the difference between a defensible outreach program and one that a single complaint can unravel. Common Mistakes When Buying B2B Data Buying a B2B dataset is easy. Buying the right one is where most teams trip up, usually in ways that only show up after the contract is signed. Chasing database size over relevant coverage. A vendor advertising 200 million contacts sounds better than one advertising 50 million, but if your accounts sit in mid-market manufacturing and the larger database is 80 percent enterprise tech, the bigger number is worthless to you. Check coverage against your actual target list, not the vendor’s total. Technographic segmentation is one method for building those target account lists more precisely. Ignoring delivery format until after signing. A team that lives in Salesforce finds out too late that a provider only ships flat files on a weekly cadence, or a data engineer finds the API has no webhook support for real-time triggers. Confirm the delivery method, whether that is API, flat files, webhooks, or MCP, fits your stack before you commit, not after the invoice arrives. Underestimating credit costs. Credit-based pricing looks cheap in a demo, right up until a team runs its actual monthly query volume through the math and finds the bill triples. Before signing, estimate how many records you will pull in a typical month and run that number against the vendor’s per-credit pricing, not the number the sales rep quoted for a light trial. Skipping compliance checks. A dataset priced well below the market rate is often built on scraped or purchased lists with no clear consent trail, and that risk transfers to you the moment you load it into your CRM. Ask about sourcing methodology before you ask about price. Never requesting a sample. Committing to an annual contract without testing a provider against a handful of your own target accounts leaves you with no basis for judging accuracy until the invoice is already paid. A vendor unwilling to hand over sample data for your own accounts is telling you something worth hearing before you sign, not after. For a deeper look at vetting vendors, see how to vet a technographic data provider for B2B sales and enrichment. The pattern across all five mistakes is the same: they surface after the contract, not during the demo. A demo shows you the best version of a product, built on whatever accounts make the vendor look good. Your own accounts, your own query volume, and your own compliance requirements decide whether a provider works for you, and none of those three things show up on a sales call unless you ask. How B2B Data Is Delivered Delivery method decides whether a dataset fits your stack, and providers vary widely in which methods they support. Four formats cover most of the market, and knowing which one matches your setup narrows a vendor shortlist fast. REST API. Built for real-time lookups and enrichment at the moment you need it, whether that is a CRM field populating on page load or an application pulling a company record mid-workflow. This is the default method most data consumers reach for, since it plugs into an existing tool without any pipeline work on your end. Flat files. Bulk delivery, typically JSONL or CSV, dropped into cloud storage on a set schedule. This is the method for warehouse ingestion into Snowflake or BigQuery, historical backfills, or any analysis that needs the full dataset instead of one record at a time. Data builders lean on this when a live API call is overkill for what they are doing. Webhooks. Push notifications that fire the moment a new signal appears for a company you are tracking, without requiring you to poll an endpoint to check. This is the format for real-time trigger workflows: alerting a rep the moment a target account posts a new job opening, or feeding an automation the instant a company news event gets detected . MCP. Model Context Protocol (MCP) is a newer standard that lets AI agents query a dataset conversationally, treating it as a callable tool instead of a fixed endpoint you have to code against ahead of time. It fits agent workflows where the query itself gets generated on the fly instead of written in advance. Not every provider supports all four, and that gap is worth checking before you sign anything. A contact database provider built around a browser extension may only offer an API and skip flat files and webhooks entirely, since its buyers are mostly reps working one record at a time. A provider built for pipeline work usually covers API, flat files, and webhooks, since data builders need all three depending on the job. Matching the method to the buyer matters more than matching it to the dataset. A data consumer generally wants a CRM connector or a simple API call, since the goal is getting clean fields into a tool that already exists. A data builder wants API access for live lookups, flat files for bulk loads, and webhooks for anything that needs to trigger downstream, often combining all three inside a single pipeline. Teams assessing niche providers for this use case may also want to review TheirStack alternatives for technographic and job data . Ask a vendor which of the four they support natively versus which require a workaround, since a method listed on a pricing page is not always the one that ships without a support ticket. Frequently Asked Questions What is a B2B data provider? A B2B data provider is a company that collects, structures, and delivers information about businesses, such as company profiles, contact records, technographic data, job signals, and news events, to sales, marketing, investment, and product teams. It supplies the underlying dataset, not the tool you view it through. What is the difference between a B2B data provider and a sales intelligence tool? A data provider supplies structured data through an API, flat files, or webhooks. A sales intelligence tool is an end-user application that displays that data in a UI, such as a filterable list or a CRM sidebar. Many sales intelligence tools are built on top of one or more data providers and do not collect the data themselves. Are there free B2B data providers? Several providers offer free tiers with limited monthly credits or record counts, including Apollo.io and PredictLeads, which includes 100 free API requests per month. A free tier lets you test accuracy and fit against your own accounts before committing, but production use across a full account list generally requires a paid plan. How do B2B data providers collect their data? Collection methods vary by category: Crawling public company websites, career pages, and news sources for company and hiring data. Using a technology detection API to identify script tags and DNS records and map the tech a company runs. Parsing job descriptions for required skills and hiring signals. Using logo recognition and optical character recognition to map business connections from case studies and partner pages. Pulling structured feeds from public filings and startup platforms. Reputable providers document their collection methods and limit sourcing to publicly available information, not scraped or purchased lists of unknown origin. PredictLeads: Company Intelligence Data Across the Full Signal Stack PredictLeads is a company intelligence data provider that tracks 129M+ companies across 195 countries, pulling structured signals from hiring activity, technology adoptions, news events, financing rounds, and business connections into a single API. Where contact database providers stop at names and emails, PredictLeads covers the layer beneath: what a company is doing right now, beyond who works there. The Job Openings dataset spans 2.8M+ companies and 279.7M+ historical records with O*NET codes, salary data, and seniority levels, so you can filter for the specific hiring signal that maps to your ICP instead of sifting through raw postings. Technology Detections cover 54,000+ technologies across 87.8M+ websites, sourced from script tags, DNS records, cookies, and job descriptions, which means tools sitting behind a login show up in the results. The News Events dataset categorizes signals from 20M+ sources into 37 event types, including receives_financing , increases_headcount_by , launches , and signs_new_client , each with a confidence score and a link back to the original source so you can judge the signal before you act on it. Data is delivered via API, flat files, webhooks, and Model Context Protocol (MCP), and every record exposes first_seen_at and last_seen_at timestamps so you can filter by recency instead of taking a vendor’s refresh claim on faith. Ready to see this in your own data? A good provider fits how your team works, not how a vendor demo was staged. Freshness, coverage depth, compliance posture, and delivery format decide whether a dataset actually moves your pipeline, and none of those show up in a record count. Use the criteria above to test any shortlist against your real accounts before you commit to a contract. Get 100 free API requests/month – no credit card, no sales call. FAQ Which B2B data provider should I use if I need technographic and hiring signals beyond contact records? If your use case is competitor displacement, integration targeting, or trigger-based outreach, you need a b2b intent data and signal provider, not a contact database. PredictLeads covers technographics across 87.8M+ websites, job openings from 2.8M+ companies, and 37 categories of structured news events, all with source-level provenance so you can judge signal quality instead of taking a black-box match on faith. How do I choose between API, flat files, and webhooks when integrating a B2B contact database provider? Use the API for real-time enrichment at the moment a record is needed, flat files for bulk warehouse ingestion into Snowflake or BigQuery, and webhooks when you need a push notification the instant a signal fires, such as a target account posting a new job opening or closing a financing round. Most data builders end up combining all three inside a single pipeline depending on the job, so confirm a provider supports all three natively before signing. What should I check before buying from any B2B database provider? Test the provider against your own target accounts before committing, not the demo accounts the vendor chose. Ask for timestamp fields like first_seen_at and last_seen_at on individual records, request documentation on sourcing methodology, and run your actual monthly query volume through the per-credit pricing math. A provider that cannot explain where a detection came from or how frequently a given dataset refreshes is asking you to trust a claim it cannot back up. Why does B2B data decay matter more than total database size when comparing top data providers? B2B data decays at roughly 22.5 percent annually, which means one in four records in a static list turns inaccurate within a year. A top b2b data provider with 200 million records and no stated refresh cadence delivers less usable coverage than a smaller provider with daily crawl cycles and exposed freshness timestamps. Database size is a marketing number; update frequency and source transparency are what determine whether the data your team acts on is still accurate when they act on it.

summary: Your strongest repowering leads may already be in your CRM, service records, and local market. Permit data, direct outreach, digital marketing, and referral partners can help identify aging systems before they fail. Solar Health Checks create a customer-friendly entry point for assessing needs and uncovering upgrade opportunities. A repeatable demand-generation system creates a steadier pipeline than relying on service calls alone. Tigo’s flexible solutions help installers serve more existing systems and support future upgrades.
body_text: TLDR Your strongest repowering leads may already be in your CRM, service records, and local market. Permit data, direct outreach, digital marketing, and referral partners can help identify aging systems before they fail. Solar Health Checks create a customer-friendly entry point for assessing needs and uncovering upgrade opportunities. A repeatable demand-generation system creates a steadier pipeline than relying on service calls alone. Tigo’s flexible solutions help installers serve more existing systems and support future upgrades. ‍ Build a Repeatable Demand-Generation Strategy Many installers assume that growing a repowering business requires finding entirely new customers. Some part of RePowering will be new customers but know that the strongest opportunities at the start may already be within reach. Past customers, service requests, aging installations, permit records, local neighborhoods, and professional referral partners can all provide qualified repowering leads. Unlike a brand-new solar sale, these homeowners already own solar and understand its value. They need a trusted professional who can evaluate the system, restore performance, and help them prepare for what comes next. A strong repowering pipeline should combine four lead-generation channels: Existing customers Local market targeting Digital and inbound marketing Strategic partnerships Together, these channels create a more predictable flow of opportunities than relying on service calls alone. ‍ 1. Start With Existing Customers If you have been installing solar for years, your customer database may be your lowest-cost and highest-converting source of repowering leads. Start by identifying homeowners who: Installed solar approximately 10 or more years ago Have aging or unsupported inverter technology Have never upgraded their monitoring Recently contacted you for service Have experienced production or communication issues Added an EV or increased household electricity use Have asked about battery storage or backup power Own systems that no longer meet their current energy needs ‍ ‍ These homeowners already know your company, which makes them easier to re-engage than a completely new prospect. Outreach may include: Email campaigns Seasonal system reminders Call campaigns with prepared scripts Service follow-ups Monitoring alerts Invitations to schedule a system assessment Battery or inverter upgrade announcements The goal is not to immediately sell equipment. It is to reopen the relationship and offer a reason to evaluate how the system is performing today. ‍ Use System-Check Language Homeowners may not understand the term repowering and contacting them with an immediate upgrade offer can feel overly promotional. A simpler entry point is to use system-check or Solar Health Check language. For example: Your solar system has been operating for more than 10 years. A Solar Health Check can help identify potential production issues, aging equipment, monitoring limitations, and potential upgrade opportunities before they become larger problems. Other customer-friendly language may include: Solar system performance check Solar health assessment System reliability review Monitoring and production check Solar equipment lifecycle review Battery-readiness assessment This language positions the installer as a service partner rather than a salesperson. It also creates a natural transition into a broader conversation about monitoring, inverter replacement, optimization, battery storage, or system expansion when those needs are identified. ‍ Create a Solar Health Check Program Rather than treating assessments as occasional promotions, installers can establish a repeatable Solar Health Check program. A basic program may include: Review of system age and available documentation Visual equipment inspection Production and monitoring review Identification of failed, aging, or unsupported components Evaluation of homeowner energy needs Battery and backup-power readiness Discussion of future expansion opportunities Written findings and recommended next steps The assessment can be complimentary, offered as a limited promotion, or provided as a paid professional service depending on the scope and the installer’s business model. Each assessment should help answer three questions: Is the system performing as expected? Does any equipment require immediate attention? What upgrades could improve the homeowner’s experience now or in the future? Every assessment creates an opportunity to uncover legitimate monitoring, inverter, optimization, storage, service, or expansion needs. ‍ 2. Target the Local Installed Base Your next repowering customer may not be in your CRM. They may live in a nearby neighborhood with a solar system installed by another company—possibly one that no longer services the system. Local market research can help installers identify these opportunities more intentionally. ‍ Use Building-Permit Data to Identify Aging Systems Local building departments often maintain permit records for residential solar installations. Depending on the jurisdiction, these records may be available through: Online municipal permit portals Public-record databases Building-department requests County or city planning offices Third-party property and permit-data services Permit records can help installers identify: When a solar system was installed Which neighborhoods have a concentration of older systems The original installer or contractor Approximate system size Properties approaching common inverter or equipment-replacement windows This information can be used to build a focused outreach list instead of marketing broadly to every homeowner in a service territory. (Installers should follow all applicable public-record, solicitation, privacy, and marketing requirements when collecting and using permit information.) ‍ Use Direct Mail to Reach Older Solar Homes Once target neighborhoods or properties have been identified, direct mail can introduce the installer’s repowering and system-assessment services. The message should focus on homeowner value rather than equipment. For example: Has your solar system been operating for 10 years or more? A Solar Health Check can help identify production issues, aging equipment, monitoring limitations, and opportunities to prepare for battery storage or future energy needs. A direct-mail campaign may promote: Solar Health Checks Inverter replacement Monitoring restoration Battery-readiness reviews Solar repair and modernization Service for systems installed by companies no longer in business Keep the message simple and include one clear action, such as scheduling an assessment or requesting a consultation. ‍ Consider Targeted Door-to-Door Outreach Door knocking can also support a local repowering campaign, particularly in neighborhoods with a high concentration of older solar systems. The approach should be educational and targeted—not a generic solar sales pitch. A simple introduction might be: “We are helping homeowners in this area evaluate older solar systems for production, monitoring, and equipment issues. We are offering Solar Health Checks for systems that have been operating for approximately 10 years or more. Would you be interested?" Representatives should be prepared to explain: Why the neighborhood was selected What the system check includes That the homeowner is not being asked to replace the entire system How an assessment can identify immediate and future needs Door-to-door outreach is most effective when combined with mailed materials, neighborhood-specific landing pages, or follow-up email campaigns. (Installers should also comply with local solicitation and licensing requirements.) ‍ 3. Strengthen Digital and Inbound Marketing When homeowners experience production problems or equipment failures, many begin with an online search. Your website should answer the questions they are already asking. Create dedicated pages and educational content around topics such as: Solar inverter replacement Solar system repair Solar system upgrades Battery retrofit Aging solar systems Solar monitoring upgrades Solar repowering Repair versus replacement Home battery installation Solar company out of business Solar system not producing Solar Health Check Educational content builds trust before the first conversation takes place and helps position your company as the local expert for existing solar systems. ‍ Use SEO, AIEO, and Paid Search Local search visibility is especially important because repowering customers often need help quickly. Optimize your website and Google Business Profile for location-based searches such as: Solar repair near me Solar inverter replacement Solar system not working Solar monitoring repair Solar battery retrofit Solar repowering company Solar service for orphaned systems SEO and AI engine optimization can help your educational content appear in traditional search results and AI-powered search experiences. Paid search campaigns can also target high-intent phrases such as: “Solar not working” “Replace solar inverter” “Solar company went out of business” “Add battery to existing solar” “Upgrade old solar system” The strongest campaigns lead homeowners to a dedicated service page with a clear Solar Health Check or assessment call to action. ‍ ‍ Stay Visible Before the System Fails The most successful repowering businesses do not wait for the phone to ring. Ongoing demand-generation activities may include: Educational email campaigns Customer newsletters Google Business Profile updates Local SEO and AIEO Paid search campaigns Social media content Community workshops Utility-bill review campaigns Direct-mail campaigns Neighborhood outreach Annual Solar Health Check promotions The goal is to become visible before the homeowner experiences a complete system failure. ‍ 4. Build Strategic Referral Partnerships Many homeowners needing repowering will not begin by calling a solar installer. They may first contact: Roofing contractors Electricians Real estate agents Home inspectors Property managers General contractors Insurance restoration companies HVAC contractors These professionals frequently encounter older solar systems during roofing projects, electrical upgrades, home sales, inspections, storm repairs, and electrification projects. Building relationships with them can create a steady source of qualified referrals. ‍ Make the Partnership Easy to Use A strong referral partnership should include more than an informal agreement to exchange names. Create a simple, repeatable process that may include: Meeting with local companies to explain repowering services Training partners to recognize potential repowering needs Establishing a referral agreement Providing a dedicated referral contact Developing co-branded homeowner materials Offering a Solar Health Check for referred customers Creating a simple online referral form Following up with the partner after the customer is served For example, a roofer preparing to replace a roof may uncover an aging inverter, damaged wiring, outdated monitoring, or a homeowner interested in battery storage. An electrician installing an EV charger may identify increased energy needs that justify additional solar capacity or storage. The easier it is for partners to identify and refer these opportunities, the more consistently the channel will produce leads. ‍ Turn Customers Into Referral Sources Satisfied repowering customers can also become strong advocates. After completing a project: Ask for a review Request introductions to neighbors with older solar systems Offer a formal referral program Share before-and-after production results Provide educational materials the homeowner can pass along Follow up about future monitoring, battery, or service needs Neighborhood referrals can be especially effective because nearby homes may have systems installed at approximately the same time and may be facing similar equipment or service issues. ‍ Don't Wait for the Phone to Ring The most successful repowering businesses actively create demand. That may include: Educational email campaigns Customer newsletters Google Business Profile optimization Local SEO Paid search campaigns Social media content Community workshops Utility bill review campaigns Annual system health check promotions The goal is to stay visible before the homeowner experiences a system failure. ‍ Why Tigo Helps You Reach More Customers One of the biggest challenges in repowering is that every existing solar system is different. Different inverter brands. Different module types. Different ages. Different homeowner goals. Rather than requiring a complete system replacement, Tigo gives installers the flexibility to modernize many existing systems through targeted upgrades. Whether the project involves restoring production, adding monitoring, improving performance, replacing an inverter, or preparing for battery storage, Tigo enables installers to recommend solutions that fit the homeowner's needs—not just a single product line. That flexibility expands the number of projects installers can pursue and helps convert more inquiries into completed repowering projects. ‍ Chapter Takeaway Finding solar repowering customers isn't about waiting for equipment to fail—it's about building a repeatable lead-generation strategy. By combining existing customer outreach, service work, local partnerships, digital marketing, and educational content, installers can create a steady pipeline of repowering opportunities. With flexible solutions that support a wide range of existing solar systems, Tigo helps installers serve more homeowners, close more projects, and build lasting customer relationships. ‍ Continue Reading Once you've built a consistent pipeline of repowering opportunities, the next step is turning those opportunities into a repeatable business. ‍ Next Chapter 6 → Launching Your Repowering Business in 90 Days

title: Eikon Therapeutics Reports Second Quarter 2026 Financial Results and Provides Clinical Updates
summary: August 13, 2026 PDF Version MILLBRAE, Calif., Aug. 13, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) — Eikon Therapeutics, Inc. (Nasdaq: EIKN) (“Eikon”), a late-stage clinical biopharmaceutical company dedicated to developing innovative medicines to...
body_text: August 13, 2026 PDF Version Eikon announced seven abstracts accepted for presentation at the European Society for Medical Oncology (ESMO) Congress 2026 highlighting progress across Eikon’s oncology portfolio, including clinical updates for EIK1001 and EIK1003 and initial clinical findings for EIK1004 and EIK1005 Presented data at the American Society for Clinical Oncology (ASCO) 2026 Annual Meeting demonstrating encouraging activity of EIK1001 combined with pembrolizumab and histology-appropriate chemotherapy for the front-line treatment of patients with advanced NSCLC in the TeLuRide-005 Phase 2 trial, and preliminary evidence that the PARP1-selective inhibitor EIK1003 could be safely combined with full-dose paclitaxel in second-line treatment of breast and ovarian cancers Progressed the TeLuRide-006 Phase 2/3 registrational trial of EIK1001 through a first interim analysis, including dose-optimization in first-line advanced melanoma Appointed Ma. Fatima “Fama” Francisco to the Board of Directors, adding decades of global commercial experience Ended second quarter of 2026 with $531.2 million in cash, cash equivalents and marketable securities MILLBRAE, Calif., Aug. 13, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) — Eikon Therapeutics, Inc. (Nasdaq: EIKN) (“Eikon”), a late-stage clinical biopharmaceutical company dedicated to developing innovative medicines to address serious unmet medical needs, today reported second quarter 2026 financial results and provided updates on its programs. “The second quarter saw meaningful acceleration of Eikon’s most important clinical programs, leading to acceptance of seven abstracts, related to all four of our current clinical candidates, for presentation at the upcoming ESMO conference in October in Madrid,” said Roger M. Perlmutter, M.D., Ph.D., Chief Executive Officer and Board Chair of Eikon Therapeutics. “These new results expand what we reported at the ASCO conference in June and advance our ability to address important unmet needs in cancer therapy. Moreover, our clinical progress reinforces the conclusion that Eikon’s unique research platform can reproducibly elucidate novel approaches towards the treatment of grievous illness.” Clinical Development Highlights EIK1001 EIK1001 is a systemically administered TLR 7/8 dual-agonist designed to stimulate both innate and adaptive immune responses to malignancy. Eikon believes that its data generated to date show that intravenous administration of EIK1001 has been generally well-tolerated, activates readily measured systemic immune responses, and can be combined with current standard-of-care for the treatment of malignant disease. Eikon will present comprehensive updated data from TeLuRide-005 ( NCT06246110 ), an ongoing open-label Phase 2 trial evaluating the safety and tolerability of EIK1001 in combination with both pembrolizumab and histology-appropriate chemotherapy for the treatment of patients with non–small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), on Monday, October 26 at the ESMO Congress 2026 in Madrid, Spain. On August 11, 2026, Eikon reported that a first interim analysis of TeLuRide-006 (NCT06697301), an ongoing global Phase 2/3 registrational trial evaluating EIK1001 in combination with pembrolizumab in the first-line treatment of advanced melanoma, was completed by an independent Data Monitoring Committee (DMC). The DMC selected, per protocol, a single dosing regimen for expansion of the trial, and recommended that the study continue as planned. On July 27, 2026, Eikon announced dosing of the first patient in TeLuRide-008 ( NCT07365319 ), a Phase 2/3 registrational trial evaluating EIK1001 in combination with both pembrolizumab and histology-appropriate chemotherapy as first-line therapy for treatment-naive patients with stage 4 NSCLC. On May 30, 2026, Eikon presented updated data at the 2026 ASCO Annual Meeting from TeLuRide-005 ( NCT06246110 ), an ongoing open-label Phase 2 trial evaluating the safety and tolerability of EIK1001 in combination with both pembrolizumab and histology-appropriate chemotherapy for the treatment of patients with non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Among other results, the presentation showed: When combined with standard-of-care therapy, EIK1001 was observed to be associated with meaningful and consistent clinical activity across PD-(L)1 tumor proportion score subgroups EIK1001 was observed to be generally well tolerated, permitting administration in the outpatient setting Durable anti-tumor activity with median response duration of greater than 11 months for the non-squamous cohort was observed A more complete characterization of these durable responses will be presented at the ESMO Congress 2026 in October. EIK1003 & EIK1004 EIK1003 and EIK1004 are highly selective PARP1 inhibitors designed to inhibit PARP1 while sparing PARP2, thereby promoting tumor regression by targeting the DNA damage response of cancer cells. EIK1004 was specifically engineered to penetrate the central nervous system (CNS), potentially expanding the utility of selective PARP1 inhibition to tumors involving the brain and CNS. Eikon believes the selectivity of EIK1003 and EIK1004 may enable the development of near full-dose combination regimens with chemotherapy, antibody-drug conjugates, or radionuclides, in earlier lines of therapy than currently possible with non-selective PARP inhibitors, and will potentially allow for more sustained therapeutic dosing during maintenance treatment. Eikon will present clinical data from its ongoing Phase 1/2 trial of EIK1003 on Friday, October 23 at the ESMO Congress 2026 in Madrid, Spain. Various trial components evaluate the safety and efficacy of EIK1003 as monotherapy or in combination with anti-cancer agents in participants with advanced solid tumors ( NCT06253130 ). The presentations will include updated data from Cohorts 1A and 1C, as well as initial data from Cohort 1B, which is specifically evaluating the safety and preliminary efficacy of EIK1003 in combination with abiraterone and prednisone for the treatment of patients with advanced prostate cancer. Eikon is also currently enrolling an additional Cohort 1D, evaluating EIK1003 in combination with paclitaxel and platinum-based chemotherapeutic regimens in patients with ovarian cancer. Site selection for Cohort 1D is completed and enrollment is ongoing. Eikon is currently evaluating two dose levels of EIK1003 monotherapy, 20 mg and 60 mg, to determine the optimal Phase 2 dose for EIK1003. Approximately 30 PARPi-naïve, HER2-negative breast cancer patients are expected to be enrolled at each dose level. Enrollment for the Part 2 dose optimization portion of the Phase 1/2 trial is ongoing. On Friday, October 23 at the ESMO Congress 2026 in Madrid, Spain, Eikon will also present, for the first time, data from an ongoing Phase 1/2 trial evaluating the safety and efficacy of EIK1004, a selective PARP1 inhibitor designed to penetrate the CNS, for the treatment of patients with ovarian, breast, prostate, and pancreatic cancers ( NCT06907043 ). Eikon believes that these results, together with data from its studies of EIK1003, will provide mutually reinforcing insights into the behavior of highly-selective PARP1 inhibitors. On May 30, 2026, Eikon presented data at the 2026 ASCO Annual Meeting from its ongoing Phase 1/2 trial evaluating the safety and efficacy of EIK1003 as monotherapy or in combination with anti-cancer agents in participants with advanced solid tumors ( NCT06253130 ), including: Updated clinical safety, tolerability and preliminary efficacy data from Cohort 1A, evaluating EIK1003 as a monotherapy for the treatment of patients with ovarian, breast, prostate, and pancreatic cancers Initial clinical safety, tolerability and preliminary efficacy data from Cohort 1C, evaluating EIK1003 in combination with paclitaxel for the treatment of patients with platinum-resistant ovarian, or breast cancer patients who are either HER2-negative, ER-positive, and hormonal therapy-experienced, or ER-negative and chemotherapy-experienced. EIK1005 EIK1005 is a novel molecular entity, designed to inhibit the Werner (“WRN”) helicase, that emerged from original research conducted in Eikon’s laboratories. Eikon believes that EIK1005 has the potential to be an effective anti-tumor agent for microsatellite instability-high (MSI-high) tumors, by producing synthetic lethality in MSI-high cells that depend upon the WRN helicase salvage pathway to maintain genome integrity. Eikon is currently evaluating EIK1005 in a Phase 1/2 trial as monotherapy and in combination with pembrolizumab in participants with advanced solid tumors ( NCT07262619 ). The first patient in this Phase 1/2 dose-escalation trial was dosed in January 2026. Preliminary safety, tolerability and pharmacokinetic data for EIK1005 will be presented on Friday, October 23 at the ESMO Congress 2026 in Madrid, Spain. EIK1006 EIK1006 is another internally-derived clinical candidate and is being investigated as a potential next-generation androgen receptor (“AR”) antagonist with activity against multiple clinically important genetic variants of AR that emerge during treatment with conventional AR blockers. Preclinically, Eikon scientists have shown that EIK1006 binds to the ligand binding domain of AR and blocks its nuclear translocation, thereby inhibiting AR transcriptional activity and downstream signaling. Eikon expects to submit an investigational new drug application (IND) for EIK1006 by the end of 2026. Key Upcoming Milestones EIK1001: Presenting full combination data from the TeLuRide-005 trial in NSCLC on Monday, October 26 at ESMO. EIK1003: Presenting updated Phase 1/2 monotherapy and combination data in patients with advanced solid tumors across Cohorts 1A, 1B and 1C on Friday, October 23 at the ESMO Congress 2026. EIK1004: Presenting initial Phase 1/2 data in patients with advanced solid tumors on Friday, October 23 at ESMO. EIK1005: Presenting initial Phase 1/2 data in patients with advanced solid tumors on Friday, October 23 at the ESMO Congress 2026. EIK1006: Expects to submit an IND by the end of 2026. Second Quarter 2026 Corporate Highlights Appointment of Ma. Fatima D. Francisco to Board of Directors Eikon appointed Ma. Fatima (“Fama”) D. Francisco as an independent director to its Board of Directors, where Ms. Francisco will also serve on the Board’s Compensation Committee. Ms. Francisco most recently served as Chief Executive Officer, Baby, Feminine and Family Care at The Procter & Gamble Company, where she led one of the company’s largest global business units. During her more than 35-year career at Procter & Gamble, she has held numerous leadership positions across marketing, innovation, commercial operations, and general management. She also serves on the Board of Directors of HP Inc. and Nestlé S.A., and previously served on the Board of Directors of Organon & Co. Second Quarter 2026 Financial Results Cash Position: As of June 30, 2026, Eikon had cash, cash equivalents, and marketable securities of $531.2 million. Eikon expects its current cash, cash equivalents, and marketable securities to fund operations into the second half of 2027. Research and Development (“R&D”) Expenses: R&D expenses were $75.5 million for the three months ended June 30, 2026, compared to $69.2 million for the three months ended June 30, 2025, an increase of $6.3 million, or 9%. Direct research and development expenses increased by $12.8 million as we advanced our clinical trial activity, and compensation costs increased by $1.7 million. These increases were partially offset by restructuring expenses and milestone payments in the prior year period and by lower occupancy costs. General and Administrative (“G&A”) Expenses: G&A expenses were $17.9 million for the three months ended June 30, 2026, compared to $40.5 million for the three months ended June 30, 2025, a decrease of $22.5 million, or 56%. The decrease was primarily due to the impairment in the year-ago period of $10.7 million of property and equipment and $10.3 million of operating lease right-of-use assets relating to properties in Hayward, California that Eikon vacated in April 2025 when the Company moved into its current corporate headquarters in Millbrae, California. Net Loss : Net loss attributable to common stockholders was $88.4 million for the second quarter of 2026, compared to $105.2 million for the prior-year period. “Our strong balance sheet enables us to continue to support an increasingly mature pipeline, including ongoing registrational studies of EIK1001 in both advanced melanoma and non-small cell lung cancer,” said Freddie Bowie, Ph.D., Chief Financial Officer. “Additional development programs to be reviewed at ESMO demonstrate our ability to execute global clinical trials across multiple indications. We remain focused on deploying capital toward opportunities that we believe have the potential to significantly enhance shareholder value over the next few years.” About Eikon Therapeutics Eikon is a late-stage clinical biopharmaceutical company dedicated to building a global, fully integrated organization developing innovative medicines to address serious unmet medical needs. Eikon’s initial focus is oncology, where it is advancing a pipeline of drug candidates that could eventually become lifesaving medicines. Eikon deploys its technology platform, including its proprietary single molecule tracking system, to develop internally derived novel therapies, while also leveraging the deep expertise of its management team to in-license promising assets. Eikon’s vision is to become a generational leader, by purposefully integrating traditional biology research with advanced engineering to develop better medicines faster. For more information, visit www.eikontx.com .
